untested: The practice command mirrors the macOS probe (lsof). The Linux equivalent (ss) isn't in the practice terminal yet.
Catching the chat app's connection while it answers depends on the answer being long enough. Not timed.
Chapter 0 says Macs and Windows laptops have a built-in window listing where each program sends data. Which window isn't confirmed; as far as I know Activity Monitor shows amounts, not destinations.
Matching a tailnet address to a machine the learner owns with tailscale status --json is not tried.
The tailnet range 100.64 to 100.127 is Tailscale's documented IPv4 range; tailnet IPv6 addresses aren't covered in the text.
stands: tailnet: Tailscale's word for your own network of machines, wherever they are.
why: Nothing beeps when a draft leaves the building. So on Wednesday Priya went and looked: which machines was her chat app talking to? One, her own box. This is the station that has to live in your head, because when it fails, it fails quietly.
mnem: Read the destinations, not the wifi icon.

steps.text: Every program that talks to another machine has a **destination**: the address it's sending to. Three kinds are yours. **Loopback** (127.0.0.1) is the machine talking to itself. A **private address** only works inside your own network; they start 10., 192.168., or 172.16 up to 172.31. Your **tailnet** is your own network across places, made with Tailscale; its addresses run from 100.64 to 100.127. Anything else is a **public address**: somebody else's machine, on the internet.
steps.hint: Three kinds are yours. Everything else isn't. That's the whole rule.

doIt.explain: I'll show you your own machine's addresses so you can see the three kinds.

steps.text: Practice run. In the practice terminal, list where a pretend chat app is sending data: `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:ESTABLISHED -c chat` Then tell me which line isn't yours.
steps.hint: Look at the address after the arrow. Is it loopback, a private address, your tailnet, or none of those?

onFail.say: Not that one. {address} is one of yours. Look for the address that isn't loopback, private or your tailnet.

steps.text: Now for real. Ask {chat_app} for something long (“Write me three paragraphs about tea.”), and while it's answering, press Check. I'll look at where {chat_app} is sending data.
steps.hint: It has to be answering while I look, so ask for something long.

doIt.explain: I can't type into {chat_app} for you. I'll tell you when to press Check.

onFail.say: Stop there. {chat_app} sent something to {address}, a public address. Don't paste anything private into it until we know why.

steps.text: Last one, and it's the red test. Tell me what this check would look like if it went wrong.
steps.hint: Picture the list with one extra line.

doIt.explain: I'll show you an example list with a public address in it.

check.question: What would it look like if your chat went somewhere it shouldn't?
check.rubric: A destination in the list that is not loopback, private or an owned tailnet machine: a public address. Better still if they say nothing beeps, so you have to look.

recap: Read the destinations, not the wifi icon.
Loopback, private addresses and your tailnet are yours. Anything else is a public address.
Nothing beeps when a draft leaves the building, so you go and look.
